title: The Son is not stronger than the Father
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὁ Κέλσος· ὅτι δὲ οὐκ ἀπὸ σκοποῦ ταῦ (τα δο) ξάζω, αὐτῶν ἐκείνων φωναῖς χρήσομαι. ἐν γάρ που τῷ οὐρανίῳ διαλόγῳ τῇδέ που λέγουσι τοῖσδε τοῖς ῥήμασιν· „εἰ ἰσχυρότερός ἐστι θεοῦ υἱὸς, καὶ κύριος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (καὶ τίς ἄλλος κυριεύσει τοῦ κρατοῦντος θεοῦ;) πῶς πολλοὶ περὶ τὸ φρέαρ, καὶ οὐδεὶς εἰς τὸ φρέαρ; διὰ τί τοσαύτην ἀνύων ὁδὸν ἄτολμος εἶ; λανθάνει σε· πάρεστι γάρ μοι θάρσος καὶ μάχαιρα.“ οὕτως οὐ τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν αὐτοῖς τὸ προκείμενον, τὸν ὑπερουράνιον θεὸν, ἀλλ᾿ ὃν ὑπέθεντο τούτου πατέρα, περὶ ὅν συνῆλθον, σέβειν, ἵν᾿ ἐπὶ προσχήματι μεγάλου θεοῦ τοῦτον, ὃν προΐστανται, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ὃν ἀποφαίνουσιν ἰσχυρότερον καὶ κύριον „τοῦ κρατοῦντος θεοῦ,“ θρησκεύωσι μόνον. ἔνθεν αὐτοῖς ἐκεῖνο τὸ παράγγελμα, τὸ μὴ „δουλεύειν“ δύο „κυρίοις,“ ἵν᾿ ἡ στάσις περὶ ἕνα τοῦτον φυλάσσηται. καὶ ἐν τούτοις δὴ πάλιν. οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ἀπὸ ποίας αἱρέσεως ἀσημοτάτης ταῦτα λαβὼν, πᾶσι Χριστιανοῖς ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν ἐγκαλεῖ· λέγω δ᾿ ἀσημοτάτης, ὡς μηδ᾿ ἡμῖν εἶναι, τοῖς πολλάκις ἐγγυμνασαμένοις πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν αἱρέσεων, φανερὰν τὴν γνώμην, ἀφ᾿ ἧς ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος εἴληφεν· εἴ γε εἴληφε καὶ μὴ ἀνέπλασεν ἢ ἀκολούθησιν προσέθηκε. σαφῶς γὰρ ἡμεῖς, οἱ λέγοντες τοῦ πάντα κτίσαντος καὶ τὸν αἰσθητὸν κόσμον εἶναι, φαμὲν τὸν υἱὸν οὐκ ἰσχυρότερον τοῦ πατρὸς ἀλλ᾿ ὑποδεέστερον. καὶ τοῦτο λέγομεν αὐτῷ πειθόμενοι, εἰπόντι τό· „ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πέμψας με μείζων μου ἐστί.“ καὶ οὐδεὶς ἡμῶν οὕτως ἐμβρόντητός ἐστιν, ὡς λέγειν· „κύριός“ ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ „ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.“ κρατεῖν δέ φαμεν τὸν σωτῆρα μάλιστα, ὅτε νοοῦμεν αὐτὸν θεὸν λόγον καὶ σοφίαν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καὶ ἀλήθειαν, πάντων μὲν τῶν ὑποτεταγμένων αὐτῷ, καθὸ ταῦτά ἐστιν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐχὶ καὶ τοῦ κρατοῦντος αὐτὸν πατρὸς καὶ θεοῦ. εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἀκόντων λόγος κρατεῖ, εἰσὶ δέ τινες ἔτι φαῦλοι οὐ μόνον ἄνθρωποι ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄγγελοι καὶ πάντες δαίμονες, τούτων φαμὲν αὐτὸν μὴ κρατεῖν μέν πω, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἑκόντες εἴκουσιν αὐτῷ· κατ᾿ ἄλλο δὲ σημαινόμενον τοῦ κρατεῖν καὶ αὐτῶν κρατεῖ (ὡς τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων φαμὲν τὸν ἄνθρωπον κρατεῖν, οὐχ ὑποτάξαντα αὐτῶν τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν, ὡς τιθασσεύσας κρατεῖ τινων λεόντων καὶ κτηνῶν δεδαμασμένων), πλὴν πάντα ποιεῖ, ἵνα καὶ τοὺς νυνὶ μὴ πειθομένους αὐτῷ πείσας κρατήσῃ καὶ αὐτῶν. καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς οὖν ψεῦδος τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ Κέλσου λεγόμενον ὡς ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀπαγγελλόμενον τό· „τίς ἄλλος κυριεύσει τοῦ κρατοῦντος θεοῦ“;
pass_a_gloss: After these things Celsus says (φημί): 'that I do not judge (δοξάζω) these things off the mark (ἀπὸ σκοποῦ), I will use (χράομαι) the voices (φωναί) of those very people. For somewhere in the Heavenly Dialogue (οὐράνιος διάλογος) they say, about here, in these words (ῥήματα): if the Son is stronger (ἰσχυρότερος) than God [or: if a Son of God is stronger], and the Son of Man (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου) is lord (κύριος) of him (and who else will lord it over (κυριεύω) the ruling (κρατέω) God?), how [are] many around the well (φρέαρ), and no one into the well? Why, accomplishing (ἀνύω) so great a road (ὁδός), are you without daring (ἄτολμος)? It escapes you (λανθάνω); for courage (θάρσος) and a sword (μάχαιρα) are present to me. Thus this is not the thing set before (προκείμενον) them, the supra-heavenly (ὑπερουράνιος) God, but the one whom they posited (ὑποτίθημι) as father of this one, around whom they came together (συνέρχομαι), to worship (σέβω), so that on the pretext (πρόσχημα) of a great God they may serve in cult (θρησκεύω) only this one whom they put in front (προΐστημι), the Son of Man, whom they declare (ἀποφαίνω) stronger than and lord of the ruling God. Thence their precept (παράγγελμα), not to be slave to (δουλεύω) two lords, so that the faction (στάσις) around this one may be guarded (φυλάσσω).' And in these again: having taken these from I know not what most obscure (ἀσημότατος) sect (αἵρεσις), he charges (ἐγκαλέω) all Christians from them; I say most obscure, so that not even to us, who have often exercised (ἐγγυμνάζομαι) against those from the sects, is the opinion (γνώμη) evident from which Celsus took these, if he took them and did not fabricate (ἀναπλάσσω) [them] or add a consequence (ἀκολούθησις). For clearly we, who say that the perceptible (αἰσθητός) world also belongs to the one who created (κτίζω) all things, say the Son is not stronger than the Father but inferior (ὑποδεέστερος). And we say this obeying (πείθομαι) him, who said: the Father who sent (πέμπω) me is greater (μείζων) than I. And none of us is so thunderstruck (ἐμβρόντητος) as to say: the Son of Man is lord of God. But we say the Saviour (σωτήρ) rules (κρατέω) most of all when we conceive (νοέω) him as God Word (θεὸς λόγος) and wisdom (σοφία) and righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) and truth (ἀλήθεια), [ruling] all things subjected (ὑποτάσσω) to him in so far as he is these, but not also the Father and God who rules him. Then, since word/reason (λόγος) does not rule the unwilling (ἄκων), and there are some still base (φαῦλος), not only men but also angels (ἄγγελοι) and all demons (δαίμονες), we say he does not yet rule these, since they do not yield (εἴκω) to him willing (ἑκών); but by another meaning (σημαινόμενον) of ruling he rules even them (as we say the man rules the irrational (ἄλογος) animals, not having subjected their ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν), as having tamed (τιθασσεύω) he rules certain lions and subdued (δαμάζω) beasts), except that he does all things so that, having persuaded also those not now obeying him, he may rule them also. According to us, then, false (ψεῦδος) is what is said by Celsus as announced (ἀπαγγέλλω) by us: who else will lord it over the ruling God?
pass_b_english: After this Celsus says: “To show that I do not judge these things wide of the mark, I will use their own words. For somewhere in the Heavenly Dialogue they say, in roughly these words: ‘If the Son is stronger than God, and the Son of Man is his lord (and who else will be lord over the God who rules?), how is it that many are around the well and no one goes into the well? Why, when you are travelling so long a road, do you lack courage? It escapes your notice; for I have courage and a sword.’ So their purpose is not to worship the God above the heavens. It is to worship the one they have supposed to be the father of this one around whom they have gathered, so that under the cover of a great God they may pay worship to this one alone whom they put forward, the Son of Man, whom they declare to be stronger than and lord over ‘the God who rules.’ Hence their command not to ‘serve two masters’ (Matthew 6:24), so that the faction around this one man alone may be kept intact.”

Here again he has taken these things from some sect, I do not know which, and a most obscure one, and on their account he accuses all Christians. I call it most obscure because not even we, who have often trained ourselves in debate against people from the sects, can make out the opinion from which Celsus has taken these things, if indeed he took them and did not make them up himself, or add some inference of his own.

For we, who say that the world of the senses too belongs to the One who created all things, say plainly that the Son is not stronger than the Father but less than he. And we say this in obedience to him, since he said: “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28). None of us is so out of his wits as to say: “The Son of Man is lord of God.”

We do say that the Saviour rules, above all when we think of him as God the Word, and Wisdom, and Righteousness, and Truth: he rules all things that have been made subject to him, in so far as he is these, but not also the Father and God who rules him. Then, since the Word does not rule over the unwilling, and there are some still wicked, not only men but also angels and all the demons, we say that he does not yet rule these, since they do not yield to him willingly. But in another sense of “rule” he rules even them, as we say that man rules the irrational animals without having brought their ruling faculty under him: so, by taming them, he rules certain lions and broken-in beasts of burden. Yet he does all things so that he may persuade even those who do not now obey him, and so rule them as well.
So, as far as we are concerned, the saying that Celsus reports as though we proclaimed it is false: “Who else will be lord over the God who rules?”

choices.choice: Celsus’s report of the ‘Heavenly Dialogue’ (an unidentified sectarian writing) runs from ‘To show’ to ‘kept intact’; Koetschau’s punctuation is followed for where Celsus’s words end and Origen’s reply begins. τῇδέ που λέγουσι τοῖσδε τοῖς ῥήμασιν is rendered ‘they say, in roughly these words’ (Celsus hedges his quotation). The opening clause εἰ ἰσχυρότερός ἐστι θεοῦ υἱὸς can be read ‘if a Son of God is stronger’ or ‘if the Son is stronger than God’; Origen’s reply (‘not stronger than the Father’) and his paraphrase ‘stronger than and lord over the God who rules’ show he takes θεοῦ as a genitive of comparison, so that reading is used. The well, road and sword sayings are obscure in the source and are rendered literally; the present participle ἀνύων is given as ‘when you are travelling’, and λανθάνει σε as ‘It escapes your notice’. περὶ ἕνα τοῦτον is rendered ‘around this one man alone’ to keep ἕνα. κύριος in Matthew 6:24 is rendered ‘masters’ as in the Gospel saying. ‘The Father who sent me is greater than I’ joins John 14:28 with the Johannine ‘who sent me’; cited to John 14:28. ὑποδεέστερον is rendered ‘less than he’ without softening Origen’s subordinationist wording. ἐμβρόντητος (‘thunderstruck’, that is, crazed) is rendered ‘out of his wits’. The titles ‘Wisdom, Righteousness, Truth’ may echo 1 Corinthians 1:30 and John 14:6; not cited inline as the allusion is not clear. The anarthrous λόγος in ‘the Word does not rule over the unwilling’ may also mean ‘reason does not master the unwilling’; capitalised as the Word because the sentence continues Origen’s description of the Saviour as God the Word. The tamed lions and beasts of burden are read as an example of rule that does not subject the ruling faculty. The editor’s supplement (τα δο) in ταῦτα δοξάζω is accepted.
τῇδέ που rendered 'in roughly these words' (hedge was dropped)
ἀνύων (present) now 'when you are travelling', not 'have come'
restored omitted ἕνα: 'this one man alone'
αἰσθητὸν κόσμον 'world of the senses', not 'visible world'
ἐμβρόντητος 'out of his wits' (English 'thunderstruck' means astonished)
taming clause recast so it reads as an example, not a contrast
closing sentence put in natural English order
